title: Variance: Covariance and Contravariance
one_liner: If a Cat is an Animal, is a List of Cats a List of Animals? Only if you cannot write to it.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Variance describes how subtyping of a type parameter relates to subtyping of the generic type. *Covariant* (`out T`): `List<Cat>` is a `List<Animal>` — safe if you only read. *Contravariant* (`in T`): a `Consumer<Animal>` is a `Consumer<Cat>` — safe if you only write. *Invariant*: neither, which is what a mutable collection must be. The rule follows from one observation: if `List<Cat>` were a writable `List<Animal>`, you could insert a Dog into a list of Cats.

**Function types are the memorable case.** A function is contravariant in its parameters and covariant in its return type. A function that accepts any `Animal` and returns a `Cat` can be used wherever one accepting a `Cat` and returning an `Animal` is expected. Fewer demands, stronger promises.

**Where the languages landed.** Java has *use-site* variance: `List<? extends Animal>` (read-only) and `List<? super Cat>` (write-only) — hence "PECS", producer extends, consumer super. Java's arrays are covariant and mutable, which is unsound and checked at runtime with `ArrayStoreException`. Kotlin and C# use *declaration-site* variance (`out`/`in`), which is tidier. Scala writes `+T`/`-T`. TypeScript infers variance structurally and is deliberately unsound for method parameters (bivariant) for ergonomic reasons — `strictFunctionTypes` fixes it for standalone function types only.

**Why it matters in practice.** This is the rule behind "why can't I pass my `List<String>` to a method taking `List<Object>`", and the reason library APIs take `? extends` on inputs. Getting it right makes an API usable; getting it wrong forces casts on your callers.

**Takeaway.** Read-only is covariant, write-only is contravariant, read-write is invariant. Everything else follows.
recall_q: When is a `List<Dog>` safely a `List<Animal>`?

title: Algebraic Data Types and Exhaustiveness
one_liner: Make the illegal states unrepresentable, then let the compiler find every place you forgot.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** *Product* types combine fields (a struct: this AND that). *Sum* types choose between variants (an enum with payloads: this OR that). The name is literal — the number of inhabitants of a product is the product of its fields' counts, and of a sum, the sum. Pattern matching over a sum type with an exhaustiveness check turns "did I handle every case?" from a code-review question into a compile error.

**Why sum types change designs.** The common alternative is a struct with several nullable fields and an implicit rule about which combinations are valid: `{status, error_message, result, retry_at}` where `error_message` is set only if `status == "failed"`. That rule lives in comments and is violated eventually. A sum type — `Pending | Succeeded(Result) | Failed(Error) | Retrying(Instant)` — makes the invalid combinations unconstructible. This is what "make illegal states unrepresentable" means concretely.

**The real win is change.** Add a variant, and the compiler lists every match that must be updated. That is a refactoring tool, not just a safety net, and it is why adding a state to a Rust or Swift enum is routine while adding one to a stringly-typed status field is an archaeology project.

**Where to find them.** Rust `enum`, Swift `enum`, Kotlin sealed interfaces, Scala/Haskell/OCaml/F# natively, TypeScript discriminated unions (switch on a literal `kind` field, with `never` in the default branch to force exhaustiveness), Java 21 sealed interfaces plus record patterns. In Go and Python you approximate with interfaces or `match` plus a linter, with no compile-time exhaustiveness.

**Takeaway.** Optional fields that are only valid together are a sum type wearing a disguise.

title: Ownership and Borrowing
one_liner: Aliasing XOR mutation, checked at compile time — and that is also a concurrency guarantee.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Every value has exactly one owner; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. You may *borrow* it: any number of shared references (`&T`) OR exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`), never both at once. Lifetimes ensure no reference outlives what it points to. The entire rule is "aliasing xor mutability", and it is enforced statically with no runtime cost.

**What it eliminates.** Use-after-free, double-free, and dangling pointers, by construction. Also iterator invalidation — mutating a collection while iterating it is a borrow conflict, not a runtime surprise. And, less obviously, data races: a `&mut T` is provably unaliased, so there is nothing to race. `Send` and `Sync` extend this across threads, which is the basis of "fearless concurrency" — the compiler rejects sharing a `Rc` between threads rather than hoping you noticed.

**The cost.** Some correct programs are rejected, because the checker is conservative. Self-referential structures, doubly linked lists and graphs are genuinely awkward; the answers are indices into a `Vec` (usually the right one), `Rc<RefCell<T>>` (moving the check to runtime), or arena allocation. Fighting the borrow checker is normally a sign the data model has unclear ownership, which is a real design problem the compiler surfaced early.

**The ideas travel.** C++ move semantics and `unique_ptr` express ownership without checking it. Swift's exclusivity enforcement and `~Copyable` are a close relative. Linear and affine types in research languages are the general form. Even in garbage-collected languages, asking "who owns this, and who may mutate it" prevents a category of bug that no GC addresses.

**Takeaway.** The borrow checker is not a memory feature with concurrency benefits; it is one rule about aliasing that happens to solve both.

title: Metric Cardinality
one_liner: One label with user IDs in it will cost more than your application.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A time series is identified by its metric name plus the full set of label values. Cardinality is the number of distinct combinations, and it is *multiplicative*: 10 endpoints x 5 status codes x 3 regions is 150 series. Add `user_id` with 100,000 values and it is 15 billion. Prometheus holds every active series in memory, so this is not a slow degradation — it is an OOM kill.

**The labels that destroy you.** User IDs, request IDs, trace IDs, session IDs, email addresses, full URL paths with embedded identifiers (`/orders/12345`), raw error messages, and timestamps. The last one is especially insidious: a label whose value changes every scrape creates a new series every scrape, forever.

**What to do instead.** Normalise paths to route templates before they become labels (`/orders/:id`). Keep high-cardinality identifiers in *logs and traces*, which are designed for them, and use metrics only for aggregatable dimensions. If you need per-user analysis, that is an analytics database, not a metrics system. Bound label values with an allowlist and an explicit `other` bucket, so an unexpected value cannot blow up the series count.

**Detecting it before it pages you.** Prometheus's `/status/tsdb` shows top series by metric and label. Alert on `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` growth rate rather than on absolute value, because the dangerous signature is a sudden slope after a deploy. And remember histograms multiply by their bucket count — one histogram with 12 buckets and 4 labels is substantial on its own.

**Takeaway.** Metrics are for aggregates and must be bounded; traces and logs are for specifics. Putting an unbounded value in a label is the most common way to take down monitoring with a one-line change.
recall_q: Which label turns a cheap metric into an expensive one?

title: Distributed Tracing and Sampling
one_liner: Head sampling is cheap and throws away the traces you needed; tail sampling keeps them and costs more.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A trace is a tree of spans sharing a trace id, propagated across service boundaries by a header (`traceparent`, per W3C Trace Context). Each span carries a start, a duration, a parent, and attributes. The value is causal: you see where a request's 900ms actually went, across ten services, instead of inferring it from ten separate latency graphs.

**Head sampling.** Decide at the root, before you know anything, usually at a fixed probability. The decision must propagate so a trace is not half-collected. It is cheap and predictable — and it discards 99% of traces, including the errors and the slow ones, which are the only ones anyone looks at.

**Tail sampling.** Buffer all spans of a trace in a collector, then decide once it is complete: keep everything with an error, everything over a latency threshold, a small random sample of the rest, plus everything touching a rare code path. You get the interesting traces *and* a statistical baseline. The cost is a stateful collector that must hold spans long enough for every service to report, with memory sized to your span rate and a timeout for traces that never complete.

**The parts people get wrong.** Not propagating context through queues and async boundaries, so the trace stops at the broker. Creating a span per function call, which buries the signal. Putting unbounded values in span attributes — fine for traces, unlike metrics, but it still costs storage. And sampling *inconsistently* across services, which produces broken traces that look like missing instrumentation.

**Takeaway.** Instrument boundaries and expensive operations, propagate context everywhere including async paths, and sample on the tail if you can afford the collector.
recall_q: What does head sampling miss that tail sampling catches?

title: SLOs and Error Budgets
one_liner: A reliability target you are allowed to miss is a decision-making tool; 100% is not.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** An *SLI* is a measurement of user-visible behaviour — the proportion of requests served successfully under 300ms. An *SLO* is the target for it: 99.9% over 30 days. The *error budget* is the complement: 0.1% of requests, which over 30 days is about 43 minutes of total unavailability. Spend it however you like. Burn it all, and the policy is that feature work stops until you are back in budget.

**Why the budget is the point.** It converts an argument about whether to ship into arithmetic. Plenty of budget left means you can take the risky deploy; budget exhausted means you cannot. It also makes the cost of reliability explicit: each extra nine multiplies engineering effort, and 100% is not a target but a refusal to make the trade — it forbids deploys, forbids experiments, and is in any case unachievable once you count your dependencies' SLAs.

**Getting the SLI right.** Measure as close to the user as you can: at the load balancer or in the client, not inside the service where failed requests never arrive. Define "good" in user terms. Exclude nothing without writing down why. A 99.9% availability SLO measured only on requests that reached your handler is measuring the wrong thing, and it will look healthy during an outage.

**Burn rate alerting.** Do not alert on "SLO violated" — by then it is over. Alert on *burn rate*: consuming budget 14x faster than sustainable over an hour is an urgent page; 3x over six hours is a ticket. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts give you both fast detection and few false positives, and they replace most threshold alerts you currently have.

**Takeaway.** Availability is a product decision with a number attached. The budget is what makes it one.
recall_q: What does an error budget authorise you to do?

title: Merkle Trees
one_liner: A tree of hashes: one root fingerprint, and a short proof for any leaf.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Hash each data block to form the leaves, then hash each pair of children to form their parent, repeatedly, up to a single root hash. Two properties follow. Any change to any block changes the root. And you can prove a specific block is in the tree by supplying `log n` sibling hashes — the verifier recomputes the path to the root and compares. That proof is small even for an enormous tree.

**What it is used for.** *Efficient diffing*: two replicas compare roots; if they differ, they descend only into subtrees that disagree, so synchronising a mostly-identical dataset costs `log n` round trips rather than a full scan. Cassandra and DynamoDB anti-entropy repair work this way, as does `rsync`'s cousin, and ZFS scrub. *Inclusion proofs*: Certificate Transparency logs let a client verify a certificate is in the public log without downloading it. Blockchains use them so a light client can verify a transaction against a block header. *Integrity at rest*: ZFS and Btrfs hash every block into a tree rooted in the superblock, which is how they detect silent corruption.

**Content addressing is the same idea.** Name a thing by the hash of its content, and identity becomes verifiable, deduplication becomes automatic, and caching becomes trivially safe because the name cannot refer to different bytes later. Git is a Merkle DAG — a commit hash covers the tree hash which covers every blob — which is precisely why history cannot be altered without every subsequent hash changing. IPFS, Nix, Bazel's action cache and every container registry rest on the same property.

**Takeaway.** When you need to compare, verify, or deduplicate large data cheaply, hash it into a tree and compare roots.
recall_q: How does a Merkle tree let two replicas find their difference without sending everything?

practice.prompt: Two replicas hold a million keys and differ in three. Design the comparison so the traffic is proportional to the differences, not to the data, and say how many round trips it takes.
practice.hint: Exchange root hashes, then descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ. Depth is log(n) with fan-out, so round trips are a handful — that is anti-entropy repair.

title: Quorums: Why R + W > N
one_liner: Overlap the read set and the write set and at least one node has the latest value.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** With `N` replicas, a write waits for `W` acknowledgements and a read queries `R` replicas. If `R + W > N`, the two sets must intersect in at least one node, so the read is guaranteed to *see* the latest acknowledged write — provided it can tell which value is latest, which needs a version. Cassandra's `QUORUM` is `floor(N/2) + 1` for both, which satisfies the inequality for any `N`.

**The tuning dial.** `W = N, R = 1` gives fast reads and slow, fragile writes (any replica down blocks writes). `W = 1, R = N` is the reverse. `R = W = quorum` balances them and tolerates `floor((N-1)/2)` failures. Dropping below the inequality — `R = W = 1` — gives you the fastest possible operations and eventual consistency, which is a legitimate choice for some data and a disaster for the rest.

**What quorums do not give you.** Not linearizability on their own: two concurrent writes to disjoint quorums can both succeed, and the system must resolve them (last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs). Not isolation, so read-modify-write cycles still race — you need compare-and-set or a lightweight transaction. And sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, which Dynamo-style systems use for availability, explicitly break the overlap guarantee: the write was acknowledged by `W` nodes, just not the *right* `W` nodes.

**The operational trap.** A quorum of 2 from 3 replicas sounds safe until you place all three in one availability zone, or until a node is "up" but 40 seconds behind. Count failure domains, not nodes.

**Takeaway.** `R + W > N` is a guarantee about *overlap*, not about correctness. You still need versioning to use the overlap, and a conflict policy for when you cannot.
recall_q: What must R + W satisfy for a quorum system to read its own writes?

title: Leases and Fencing Tokens
one_liner: A lock you can lose without noticing needs a token the storage layer will reject.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A distributed lock is really a *lease*: it expires. A client that acquires it may be paused — by a GC pause, a VM migration, a slow disk, a network partition — for longer than the lease, during which the lock service hands it to someone else. The first client wakes up believing it still holds the lock and writes. Two writers, no error anywhere, corrupted data.

**The fix is not a better lock.** No timeout tuning closes this, because the pause can always exceed the timeout. The fix is a *fencing token*: the lock service issues a monotonically increasing number with each grant, the client includes it in every write, and the **storage system** rejects any write carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen. The holder that woke up late is fenced out by the resource itself.

**The consequence most people miss.** This means the resource must participate. A lock in front of a dumb blob store does not make writes safe; the store has to check the token. This is why `zxid` in ZooKeeper, `mod_revision` in etcd, and epoch numbers in Kafka's leader election all exist, and why HDFS's NameNode fencing is a real feature rather than an afterthought.

**Related mechanics.** A lease needs renewal well before expiry, and a clean *abdication* path when renewal fails — the holder must stop work *before* the lease expires, not when it notices. Clock skew makes absolute-time leases unsafe; prefer durations measured locally. And "Redlock" style multi-node locking does not solve the pause problem either, which was the substance of the Kleppmann/Antirez exchange worth reading in full.

**Takeaway.** If losing the lock silently would corrupt data, you need a token the storage layer enforces — not a lock, a fence.
recall_q: What failure does a lease alone fail to prevent, and what fixes it?

title: The Exactly-Once Illusion
one_liner: You cannot get exactly-once delivery. You can get at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which is what people mean.
body_md:
**The mechanism of the impossibility.** A sender cannot distinguish "the message was lost" from "the acknowledgement was lost". It must choose: resend (at-least-once, duplicates possible) or not (at-most-once, loss possible). There is no third option, and adding more acknowledgements only moves the uncertainty to the last one — this is the two-generals problem, and it is a proof, not an engineering gap.

**What "exactly-once" products actually sell.** Exactly-once *effects*, achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with deduplication at the consumer. Kafka's transactions give you atomic read-process-write *within Kafka*: the consumer offset commit and the output production land in one transaction, so a reprocessed batch does not double-emit. That is genuinely useful and genuinely not delivery semantics. The moment your side effect leaves the system — charging a card, sending an email, writing to an external database — you are back to needing idempotency.

**How to actually get the effect.** Make the operation naturally idempotent (setting a value rather than incrementing it). Or dedupe on a stable message id, recorded *in the same transaction* as the side effect — that is the inbox pattern, and the transactional coupling is the whole trick. Or make the operation commutative and associative so order and repetition do not matter, which is the CRDT answer.

**The accounting corollary.** Counters are the hard case: `balance = balance + 10` applied twice is wrong, and applied zero times is also wrong. Model it as an append-only ledger of uniquely-identified entries and compute the balance, and duplicates become detectable rather than destructive.

**Takeaway.** Stop trying to deliver exactly once. Make processing idempotent, and the delivery guarantee stops mattering.
recall_q: What is actually achievable instead of exactly-once delivery?

title: Zero-Copy I/O
one_liner: Every copy between kernel and user space is pure overhead when you are only moving bytes.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Serving a file the naive way costs four copies and four context switches: disk to page cache (DMA), page cache to your user buffer (`read`), user buffer back to a socket buffer (`write`), socket buffer to the NIC (DMA). If your process never looks at the bytes, two of those copies and two switches are waste. `sendfile()` transfers directly from the page cache to the socket inside the kernel. With scatter-gather DMA support the data never leaves the page cache at all — the NIC reads from it directly, leaving true zero copies.

**Where it is already working for you.** Kafka's throughput story is substantially this: `sendfile` from the log segment straight to the consumer socket, which is also why *any* feature requiring the broker to inspect or transform messages costs so much. Nginx's `sendfile on`. `splice()` and `tee()` for pipe-to-pipe movement. `io_uring` with registered buffers for a more general version. And `mmap` for read paths, with the caveat that page faults are synchronous and unpredictable.

**When it does not apply.** The moment you need to touch the bytes — TLS encryption, compression, parsing, transformation — you need them in a buffer you can address. Kernel TLS (kTLS) exists to claw back the TLS case specifically. Note that this is also why enabling TLS changed your throughput profile more than expected.

**The user-space analogue.** Within your own code, the same principle is "do not copy to parse": slices and views over one buffer rather than substrings, `bytes.Buffer` reuse, Netty's `CompositeByteBuf`, Arrow's columnar layout for zero-copy IPC, and `Cow<'_, str>` in Rust. The cheapest copy is the one you do not make.

**Takeaway.** When a system's job is to move bytes rather than understand them, copies are the budget. Count them.

title: Blocking, epoll, and io_uring
one_liner: Three answers to 'how do I wait for ten thousand sockets', each solving the previous one's bottleneck.
body_md:
**Thread-per-connection.** A blocking `read()` per connection, one thread each. Simple and genuinely fast at low connection counts, but each thread costs a stack and a scheduling slot, and the context-switch cost dominates in the thousands. This is the C10K problem.

**Readiness notification: select, poll, epoll, kqueue.** Register many file descriptors with the kernel and ask which are *ready*, then do non-blocking reads on those. `select` and `poll` are O(n) per call because you resubmit the whole set every time; `epoll` (Linux) and `kqueue` (BSD/macOS) keep the set in the kernel and return only the ready ones, making it O(ready). This is the foundation of nginx, libuv/Node, Netty, and Go's netpoller. Its limit: readiness tells you an operation *would not block*, so you still pay two syscalls per operation, and it never worked properly for regular file I/O — which is why "async" runtimes historically ran file reads on a thread pool.

**Completion notification: io_uring (and IOCP).** You submit *operations* to a shared ring buffer and collect completions from another, with no syscall required in the common case. It batches, supports real asynchronous file I/O, handles `open`/`close`/`accept`/`statx`, and can chain dependent operations so a read-then-write needs no round trip to user space. The gains are largest for small, numerous operations — exactly where syscall overhead was the cost. The downsides are real: a large kernel attack surface (several distributions restrict it), a steeper API, and a kernel version floor.

**Takeaway.** Readiness models ask "can I go now?"; completion models say "do this and tell me when it is done". That difference is why io_uring removes a syscall per operation and finally makes file I/O asynchronous.
recall_q: What distinguishes non-blocking I/O from asynchronous I/O?

title: Data-Oriented Design
one_liner: The cache, not the CPU, is the constraint — so lay out data the way you traverse it.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A main-memory access costs on the order of 100ns; an L1 hit costs about 1ns. A modern core can retire several instructions per cycle, so a cache miss is hundreds of wasted instruction slots. Performance is therefore mostly about memory access patterns, and a layout that matches your traversal order beats a cleverer algorithm on the wrong layout.

**Array of structs vs struct of arrays.** `Particle[]` with position, velocity, colour and mass interleaved means a loop that only updates positions still drags every other field through cache — you might use 12 of every 64 bytes fetched. Splitting into parallel arrays (`float[] x, y, z`) means every byte fetched is used, and the loop vectorises. This is the single highest-leverage transformation in hot loops, and it is why ECS architectures in game engines and columnar formats in analytics databases look the way they do.

**The companion techniques.** Sort data to make branches predictable — a mispredicted branch costs 15–20 cycles, and a sorted array can make the same loop several times faster with no algorithmic change. Replace pointer-chasing structures with indices into contiguous arrays (a linked list is a cache miss per node). Batch by type so the branch is outside the loop rather than inside it. Prefer `Vec<T>` over `Vec<Box<T>>`. Pack hot fields together and move cold ones out of the struct.

**The discipline it implies.** Measure before and after, with cache-miss counters (`perf stat -e cache-misses,LLC-load-misses`) rather than intuition, because the wins are large and the predictions are unreliable. And apply it only to hot paths — this style trades readability for throughput, and that trade is wrong almost everywhere.

**Takeaway.** Ask what the loop touches, then make exactly that contiguous.

title: Canary and Blue-Green Deploys
one_liner: Two different bets: blue-green swaps everything at once, a canary risks a small slice.
body_md:
**Blue-green.** Run two identical environments. Deploy to the idle one, verify it, then switch all traffic over at the load balancer. Rollback is another switch, so it is fast and complete. The costs: double the infrastructure during the window, no gradual exposure (a bug that passes smoke tests hits 100% of users instantly), and database schema compatibility becomes mandatory because both versions may be live across the cutover — see expand/contract.

**Canary.** Send a small fraction — 1%, then 5%, then 25% — to the new version while watching metrics, and promote or roll back based on what you see. You risk only that fraction, and you get real production signal that no staging environment can give you. The costs: both versions run simultaneously for a long time, so they must tolerate each other's data and messages; and you need enough traffic for 1% to be statistically meaningful within a useful time window.

**What makes a canary work rather than theatre.** Automated analysis comparing canary against a *control group running the old version on fresh instances* — not against yesterday's baseline, because that conflates the deploy with time-of-day effects. Clear promote/abort criteria defined before you start (error rate, latency percentiles, saturation, plus a couple of business metrics). Sticky routing so a user does not flip between versions mid-session. And a bake time long enough to catch slow leaks: memory growth and connection exhaustion do not show up in five minutes.

**The composition that works.** Deploy dark (new code, feature off), canary the rollout, then ramp the *feature flag* separately. Separating "new binary is running" from "new behaviour is on" means a bad feature does not require a rollback, and that is the single biggest reduction in deploy risk available.

**Takeaway.** Blue-green buys instant rollback; canary buys early detection. Flags let you have both and ramp behaviour independently of code.
recall_q: What makes a canary a canary rather than a slow rollout?

title: Strangler Fig
one_liner: Replace a legacy system by intercepting its traffic one route at a time, never by rewriting it.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Put a facade — a proxy, gateway, or router — in front of the legacy system so all traffic flows through something you control. Implement one capability in the new system and change the facade to route that path to it. Repeat. The legacy system shrinks as the new one grows, and eventually nothing routes to it and you delete it. Named for the fig that grows around a host tree until the tree is gone.

**Why the alternative fails.** The big-bang rewrite requires you to reach feature parity with years of accumulated, undocumented behaviour before you can ship anything — during which the old system keeps changing, so the target moves. You carry all the risk to one cutover date, and you cannot deliver value until it arrives. The strangler delivers continuously and lets you stop halfway with something coherent, which is the real option value.

**The hard part is data, not code.** Routing requests is easy; two systems owning overlapping state is not. Options, roughly in order of preference: give the new service its own tables and keep the legacy read-only for that data; replicate one way with CDC and accept defined lag; or write to both during a transition with reconciliation, which is the expensive one and should be time-boxed. Decide the direction of truth per entity, in writing, and make it visible in the code.

**The techniques that make it practical.** Branch-by-abstraction inside the old codebase for logic you cannot route around. Dark launching: send real traffic to the new implementation, compare its output against the old one, and discard it — this finds behaviour differences before any user sees them. Verify-and-fallback for riskier paths.

**The failure mode to watch.** Stalling at 70%. Whatever remains is the gnarliest part, the funding dries up, and you now operate two systems forever. Budget for the deletion explicitly and treat the old system's removal as the deliverable.

**Takeaway.** Incremental replacement behind a facade, with per-entity data ownership decided up front and a commitment to finish.
recall_q: How does a strangler fig migration avoid a big-bang cutover?

title: Binary Search on the Answer
one_liner: If you can check an answer cheaply, you can search for it — no array required.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Binary search does not need a sorted array. It needs a *monotone predicate*: some `ok(x)` that is false for every x below a threshold and true for every x at or above it. The array case is just `ok(i) = a[i] >= target`. Once you see the predicate, the search space can be capacity, time, a rate limit, a budget — anything orderable.

**The shape that does not have off-by-one bugs.** Keep one invariant: `lo` is always a value where the predicate is false (or one below the range) and `hi` is always a value where it is true. Loop while `lo + 1 < hi`, set `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, and move whichever bound the test justifies. On exit `hi` is the answer. Writing `(lo + hi) / 2` instead overflows on large bounds — the bug that sat in `java.util.Arrays.binarySearch` for nine years.

**Where it shows up in real work.** Sizing a connection pool against a latency SLO. Finding the largest batch that fits a timeout. Picking a compression level under a CPU budget. Capacity planning of any kind: `can we serve this load with N machines?` is monotone in N, so you binary search N instead of guessing. Percentile estimation over a histogram is the same move.

**The cost model.** `O(log range)` calls to the predicate, so the predicate is where all the time goes. If `ok(x)` is a full simulation costing O(n), the total is `O(n log range)` — still usually far better than trying every value. If the predicate is a real experiment rather than a function, remember that it must be *deterministic*, or the search converges on noise.

**Takeaway.** When a problem asks for a minimum or maximum that satisfies a condition, stop trying to construct the answer. Ask whether you can test one.
